inline.s: When for an instant our thought comes to rest and is yet clearly aware — what is this? Apart from this, to seek Buddha-nature anywhere else is to find nothing. Do not suppose that because one lacks the three insights and the six superknowledges, and lacks the same spiritual powers and functions as all the Buddhas, one is therefore not awakened, not a Buddha. It is not that in a single lifetime one can be endowed with the Buddhas’ great powers and functions. To awaken to the Way for the first time is only like a newborn babe: though the babe lacks the strength of a grown man, cannot work, cannot walk, cannot eat, and must be fed and carried, you cannot say it is not a person. One newly awakened to the Way is a Buddha in the cause-ground. You must be aware at every moment and guard it at every moment. Maintain it closely and continuously, and let it diminish again and again, letting your habitual tendencies and afflictions lessen day by day; then this babe grows up, becomes a grown man, and is complete in all powers and functions. To apply effort once the original self is understood is what is called true cultivation after enlightenment. If one has not realized it, then it is blind practice and wild striving. For instance, if you recite the Buddha-name without awakening to the original self, you are reciting a Buddha outside the mind. We who recite the Buddha-name must understand that reciting Amitabha is to rouse our own true master, to call our own master to wake again and again — not to sink into forms and colors, not to be swept along by circumstances, not to cherish the common feelings of grasping and clinging. Only by doing so can you succeed. This is of the utmost importance!

But one may take emptiness-and-stillness as the self-substance, not acknowledging the physical body; take the numinous knowing as self-mind, not acknowledging delusive thoughts.” We must understand that this physical body, this flesh, this husk, is not ourselves. Our true essence is that which is empty and still — an unmoving, unshaking, neither coming nor going, neither being born nor dying thing — not this husk. This husk changes slowly, from youth to age, from age to death. Do not acknowledge this body; the body is the form-body, and this form-body is not oneself. By no means should we acknowledge this form-body as self; rather, acknowledge emptiness-and-stillness as self. That Buddha-nature which is empty and yet still, neither coming nor going, neither moving nor shaking, is our very self! “Take the numinous knowing as self-mind, not acknowledging delusive thoughts.” What is a delusive thought? To have attachment is a delusive thought. A thought arises and the mind is fixed upon it; with abiding, with clinging, this is a delusive thought. When a thought arises without abiding and without clinging, that is the true mind’s wondrous function. This clear, luminous knowing is the true mind; it is not dead. To sit motionless, to suppress thought so hard that not a single thought arises, is to turn into a great boulder, a great log. Therefore the luminous knowing, unattached, ungrasping, without love or aversion, is the true mind’s wondrous functioning. To abide, to discriminate — that is deluded feeling. But one point must be made clear: it is not that one may not discriminate, but that one discriminates without abiding. That this man is good I know; that that man is bad I too am clear — it is not that one fails to distinguish good and bad and becomes a muddlehead. Is a muddlehead the true mind? Not at all. One should know good and bad, and yet remain without aversion or attachment, without grasping or discarding. It is not that seeing a good person one delights, and seeing a bad person one recoils. The bad person too we do not abandon — why? We should teach him, pity him, help him, and turn him around; only that is right. The true mind is just this. Therefore the true mind and the deluded mind are quite easy to distinguish. At every moment let us not acknowledge the deluded mind as self; we must know that the numinous knowing, clear and unattached to form, is the true mind; the moment there is attachment, a nest is formed, and one falls into form.

If delusive thoughts arise, do not follow them. Then at the very time of death, karma can no longer bind you.” This speaks of the moment of death — what happens at death? To be able to take rebirth self-masterfully at the end of life, one must have done the practice in daily life of “if delusive thoughts arise, do not follow them.” If our delusive thoughts are not yet entirely eradicated, and in an instant a delusive thought arises again, we must be aware at once and not chase after it. If a delusive thought is strong, and awareness alone cannot cut it off, then quickly recite the Buddha-name, or hold a mantra; or raise the huatou (head-word) and ask where this delusive thought comes from, thereby dissolving it. If you have followed the delusive thought far gone before you realize it, then it is already too late. The speed of awareness and the quickness of removal are matters of the strength of one’s practice. It is like the difference between a candle flame and an electric light. At first it illuminates, but further on the light is dim; a delusive thought arises and only much later do we become aware of it — this is the candle flame. When the practice has become fully mature, the moment a thought arises we see it — like a strong light shining before us, so that every pit and hollow is clearly visible, and one walking the night road does not fall into a pit or a trench — this is the electric light. This reaches the stage of stillness that constantly illumines, and illumination that is constantly still; one no longer deliberately attends to the illumination, but it illumines of itself. In this matter there is a great depth of difference in the levels of practice.

In doing our practice we must be aware at every moment, practicing closely and continuously. If in a single day of twenty-four hours we practice for only an hour or two and are lax for the other twenty-two, that is far too lazy, and it is difficult for the practice to advance. Therefore we must practice constantly, always aware, within the four deportments of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; only then can the practice advance.

Again, if delusive thoughts arise, do not follow them along. It is not that because a certain delusive thought seems good one runs after it. Someone has a fine dream, and when he wakes cannot bear to let it go, still thinking of it. The dream scene is originally false — why cling to it? If in a dream you were emperor, are you truly an emperor? If in a dream you gained a great treasure, did you truly gain a treasure? To cling to it, is that not folly! How foolish people are!

Master Guifeng, with bitter heart and kind words, tells us: if delusive thoughts arise, do not follow them, do not run after them. If we truly accomplish this, then “at the very time of death, karma cannot bind you.” To bind is to tie up. All beings run along with karma! Those with good karma rise to heaven; those with evil karma fall into hell. If one can truly accomplish that when a delusive thought arises one does not follow it, then at that time karma cannot tie you, and you are free.

Though there is an intermediate state, where one goes is free; in heaven or among humans, one may dwell as one wishes.” One who has truly awakened to the Way has no intermediate body, and one who is born in the Western Pure Land likewise has no intermediate body. What is the intermediate state? It is when the former body has perished and the later body has not yet arisen: the former husk has broken, and one has not yet been conceived into the later husk; the body of that intermediate state between the two is the intermediate body. This intermediate body is dominated by the wind element, so it possesses the five superknowledges. Of the six superknowledges it lacks the knowledge of the extinction of defilements; it possesses only a small measure of the five superknowledges, not the five great superknowledges of a Buddha. The intermediate body has a portion of the five superknowledges, so it has the superknowledge of magical powers: wherever the parents are who have affinity with it, a thousand li or ten thousand li away, it drifts there in an instant. It has the heavenly eye, so it can see even a thousand li or ten thousand li away. Those born in the Western Pure Land have gone there and have no intermediate body. Those who fall into hell likewise have no intermediate body. Once fallen into hell, where would there be an intermediate body? The other realms all have an intermediate body. “Though there is an intermediate state, where one goes is free” — if one truly accomplishes that when a thought arises one does not follow it, then karmic hindrances cannot grasp you, cannot tie you, cannot obstruct you. Wherever you wish to go, you go there, free and self-masterful. “In heaven or among humans, one may dwell as one wishes” — either in heaven or in the human world, one may dwell as one wishes. This is the most elementary level of practice: before one can cut off delusive thoughts, when a delusive thought arises, one is able not to follow it. When practice reaches this point, even though one still has an intermediate body, one can still be free and self-masterful. But if a delusive thought arises and one runs after it, then it is ruined, and one cannot be free. So this is the most elementary step, the lowest grade.

If the thoughts of love and aversion are already extinguished, one no longer receives a body subject to birth-and-death in stages.” Love is affection, liking; aversion is hatred, dislike. The mind of love and hatred is gone. It is not that this being good I take, that being bad I discard. For all things are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, shadows — what ground is there for good and bad? What is there to love or hate? This must truly be accomplished. If someone merely explains it to you and you can do it for a while, but when you are alone you still have feelings of love and aversion, then it still does not count. When the thoughts of love and aversion are extinguished — “extinguish” means to destroy, to make vanish — the thoughts of love and aversion are done away with, and one no longer receives birth-and-death in stages; one leaves the round of birth and death. Of course, there remains still the attachment to dharmas that must be removed.

Then of oneself one can turn the short into the long, the coarse into the subtle.” This speaks of function. Such a person can transform self-masterfully: the short can become long, the coarse and poor can become subtle and exquisite. He can transform; even the six realms of transmigration can be transformed into spiritual wonders; all things are transformed. Do you not often ask: “Where has my practice reached?” You may inspect and verify it for yourself. First, is it that delusive thoughts arise and you no longer follow them? If you can do this, then wherever you go you are free. Further, if you can extinguish the mind of love and aversion, without liking, without disliking, all equal, equal, and equal again, then birth-and-death in stages is eliminated, and you can transform self-masterfully.

To advance still further: “If the subtle streaming is all extinguished, and only the perfect-enlightened great wisdom alone stands luminous, then one can respond to conditions and manifest hundreds of thousands of koṭis of transformation-bodies, delivering beings with affinity — this is called a Buddha.” This is the supreme vehicle. In our practice we must bring it about that the subtle streaming is wholly extinguished, that the seeds of the subtle delusive thoughts are all eliminated, and thoroughly realize the state of “only the perfect-enlightened great wisdom, standing luminous and alone,” thereby perfecting the fruit of Buddhahood. If in this life, having seen the nature, we break through the first barrier, and then train ourselves amid the affairs of the world, diligently eliminating our habitual tendencies, until we are free whether in favorable or adverse circumstances, unhindered in all directions; after breaking the second barrier, then advance further upward, and eliminating the subtle streaming entirely, we emit a great radiance that illumines all ten directions without obstruction. You need not seek supernatural powers; supernatural powers will of themselves come to you. Thus one can respond to conditions and manifest hundreds of thousands of koṭis of transformation-bodies, delivering beings with affinity. Buddhas and bodhisattvas respond to conditions in this way, appearing according to the occasion, to deliver beings.

There are three kinds of mind-born bodies: first, the mind-born body of the bliss of samādhi; second, the mind-born body of the awareness of the nature of dharmas; third, the mind-born body of all kinds complete, without doing. Sitting in meditation, entering deeply into samādhi and deep chan concentration, one can bring forth the mind-born body of the bliss of samādhi. The mind-root is the seventh consciousness; the body that the seventh consciousness, the mind-root, manifests is called the mind-born body. It transforms from few to many, and finally all hundreds of thousands of koṭis of transformation-bodies are complete. “All kinds complete, without doing” — mountains, rivers, the great earth, towers, pavilions, and so forth can all be manifested and transformed. To what extent must the practice reach before the subtle streaming can be cut off? What is called subtle is that we cannot see it now; only after practicing deeply and entering the samādhi of Vajrasattva can we see it: ah, so many subtle delusive seeds, moving so violently! Knowing that these are moving, we dissolve them until they no longer move; but to have still a “not moving” is itself not enough — that “not moving” too must be eliminated. Break through it, and the realm of consciousness is broken. Consciousness is the last of the five aggregates; when the aggregate of consciousness is broken, one is accomplished. So in our practice and cultivation, we must truly cultivate after enlightenment. But if you have not awakened to the true mind and understood the principle, how can you cultivate? Therefore knowing the true mind and understanding the principle is most important, that is, the mind-born body of the awareness of the nature of dharmas is most important.

Today I have again explained the meaning of form and emptiness, and once more reaffirmed the importance of recognizing the true mind (correct view): why it is necessary to recognize the true mind, and I have spoken of where a practitioner finally goes at the moment of death. You should practice in this way at every moment — just “always be aware, and let it diminish again and again.” At every moment we should be aware and observe: oh, a thought has come. Oh, I have again attached to a form. Oh, a delusive thought has arisen. Quickly do not move, do not follow it — this is called “letting it diminish again and again.” Do not speak of sudden enlightenment complete in one go; that is probably not easily accomplished, is it? Do we not often hear people say, “Oh, how is it I still have so many thoughts?” You see, to wipe away thoughts completely in one stroke is no easy matter; therefore one must always be aware and let it diminish again and again. How then do we examine whether we are making progress? One should look back and compare with the past: how formerly one grasped and fretted; now somewhat less than before, and the heart much more calm and even — that is progress. Having progress is good, for knowing there is progress strengthens faith. In the course of our practice, when the body grows warm and radiance appears, these are good phenomena. But we must not chase after them; the moment we do, it is finished — that is attachment, that is deluded thought and feeling.

After enlightenment, in our practice we should let things be natural, like a flowing stream passing by, gush, gush, gush — not lingering, not attaching, not running after states, not following the flow of delusive thoughts; letting our idle thoughts and habitual tendencies diminish again and again until they are utterly wiped away, then we can accomplish the great Way. This is the secret of the practice; therefore, without recognizing the true mind, cultivation is of no avail; recognizing the true mind but not knowing the secret, one cannot accomplish.

blocks.text: 10. The Essential Meaning of the Pure Land

inline.s: When we recite Amitabha Buddha, we are awakening our own mind, not beseeching a Western Amitabha Buddha. When we make the vow to be born in the Western Pure Land, we are of one mind with Amitabha Buddha; it is both self-power and other-power. We should understand that the function of reciting the Buddha-name is to use the Buddha’s sacred name to wash away the defilement and affliction in our hearts, to use the Buddha’s radiance to illumine us and dispel our karmic hindrances. Then, when we make the vow to be born in the West, we can be born in the Western Pure Land. How is one born there? It is to sever the root of love. If one can do this, success is certain. If you still cling to this world, however much you insist “I have other-power, I have other-power, I have other-power,” in the end you cannot be born in the Western Pure Land. Because your root of love is not severed and you are still attached to this Saha world, how can you depart? In fact, other-power is self-power, and self-power is other-power; self and other are not two. To split self and other into two is wrong. In our practice we must cultivate both — that is, to combine self-power with other-power. Relying only on other-power, self-power does not rise, and it is useless. For your delusive thoughts are not eliminated and you cling to this Saha world, so other-power cannot pull you along. If Buddhas and bodhisattvas could pull, they would have pulled everyone long ago. How do the Buddhas and bodhisattvas receive and guide beings to the West? They shine a light upon you. If you do not open your eyes, they shine on you, but you cannot see their light — what use is it? Therefore Master Yongming Yanshou says: our mind is like a basin of water, and Buddhas and bodhisattvas are like the moon in the sky. When Amitabha Buddha shines his light upon us, if our mind-water is clear, then the reflection of the moon can appear — this is the mutual response of feelings and the Way, other-power and self-power combined in one. If our mind-water is a basin of filthy water, then the moon cannot be reflected. It is not that the Buddha does not shine upon you; the Buddha has no such unequal heart, the Buddha illumines universally. It is your mind that is defiled. Therefore the blind do not see light, and filthy water does not reflect the moon. This is entirely our own misunderstanding; it is not that the Buddha does not illumine us. Therefore we must cultivate both — there is other-power and there is self-power.

To be born in the Western Pure Land, one must let go of everything and recite the Buddha-name earnestly and sincerely: “Amitabha Buddha, Amitabha Buddha…,” awakening the self-mind. The other mind is the self-mind, and the self-mind is the other mind, fused into one, so that mind and Buddha interpenetrate. At the moment of death, that Buddha appears before you. This “moment of death” not only refers to the time when one is dying, but also to the time when the root of birth and death is cut off. What is the time when the root of birth and death is cut off? It is when our deluded feelings and deluded thoughts and deluded mind die down and are cut off — this is the moment of death. For the root of our birth and death is deluded feeling, deluded thought, deluded mind. Where did we originally have birth and death? It is all these deluded feelings, deluded thoughts, and deluded mind clinging to forms, creating karma and receiving retribution, thus transmigrating through the six realms in false birth and death. When we single-mindedly recite the Buddha-name, and practice matures, when the season and conditions arrive, “pa” — in an instant the deluded feeling, deluded thought, and deluded mind are cut off, and this root of birth and death comes to an end. “At the moment of death, that Buddha appears before you” — “that Buddha” is that Buddha, is Amitabha Buddha, is our self-nature Buddha; the self-nature Buddha is Amitabha Buddha. “Appears before you” means the original nature manifests — this is called “when the flower opens, one sees the Buddha and realizes non-birth.” When the heart-flower opens and one sees the self-nature Buddha, this is enlightenment. “Realizing non-birth”: when enlightened, one sees the unborn, undying original nature! This is the Pure Land school — the true Pure Land school! We must never push the great matter of birth and death onto Amitabha Buddha alone. Do not say this is other-power, and if you, Amitabha Buddha, do not save me, it is your fault, not mine. That is wrong. If your own deluded feeling, deluded thought, and deluded mind are not cut off, how can that Buddha appear before you, and how can you realize non-birth? This is entirely your own fault; how can you blame Amitabha Buddha?

The Pure Land school is the Chan school, and the Chan school is the Pure Land school. This is what the great sages of old taught: “Chan is the Chan of the Pure Land; the Pure Land is the Pure Land of Chan.” Chan is the Pure Land, and the Pure Land is Chan. They cannot be split into two, cannot be seen as two matters; they truly are one matter. For instance, Master Yongming Shou was a Chan master — how did he become a great patriarch of the Pure Land school? Master Lianchi too was a Chan master; Master Chewu also was a Chan master — how did they all become great patriarchs of the Pure Land school? Chan and the Pure Land originally breathe through one nostril; it is only people of later times, not understanding the principle, who forcibly divide Chan from the Pure Land. When we make the vow to be born in the West, our mind must be sincere, free of doubt. The vow must be earnest — not a mere mouthing of words, but with real action. If mind has flights and practice is scattered, it cannot be saved. Morning in this, evening in this, wandering in this, distressed in this, never forgetting at any moment — then you are near attaining the Way. So too with the Chan practitioner: he must always be aware, always protect, tending the huatou. So too with us who cultivate the esoteric path: I say again and again that in practicing the Heart-Mind method one cannot rely solely on the two hours of seated meditation; the contemplation after meditation is most important, and the post-meditation is even more important than the meditation itself. In the post-meditation, we train our mind amid circumstances: see whether your mind is empty or not — this is the most important move.

I often hear people say: Oh, today I was angry to death, so-and-so is this, so-and-so is that. Let me ask you — are you a person of Buddhist faith? What is there still to be angry about? Having taken up Buddhism, you should have no anger. All things are empty; no person, no self, no self, no other — what is there to be angry about? If you still have anger, then you have not practiced Buddhism, have not been aware at every moment, have not trained your mind amid circumstances. The more adverse the circumstances and the more infuriating the affairs, the more they train you — see whether you are still angry! If you are still angry, you have not trained, and without training how can you accomplish Buddhahood? Adverse circumstances are in fact good situations, training you to see whether you are awakened. Do not say that adverse circumstances are bad; bad or not depends on whether you are awakened, on whether you can use this situation to train yourself. We who study Buddhism, whether we practice Chan, the Pure Land, or the esoteric path, must at every moment train our mind amid circumstances. Failing this, there is absolutely no achievement.

Our wondrous, luminous true mind belongs neither to being nor to non-being. Say it exists, and yet there is no form to see, no sound to hear; say it does not exist, and in speech and silence, movement and stillness, walking, standing, sitting, and lying — there is not one thing that is not its functioning. The ancients compared it to “the taste of salt in the sea,” “the azure pigment in paint” — though it cannot be seen directly, its substance truly is not absent. Śākyamuni Buddha tells us that it is a great storehouse of true emptiness and wondrous being, of wondrous being and true emptiness. What is called true emptiness is distinct from callow emptiness and annihilating emptiness; because of wondrous being, it is empty and yet not empty. What is called wondrous being is distinct from false being or substantial being; because of true emptiness, it is being and yet not being, not being and yet being. Next, from the standpoint of form and function, it too is neither being nor non-being, neither non-being nor being. Say it does not exist, and yet forms and colors stand arrayed before us, and its wondrous functions are as many as the sands of the Ganges; say it exists, and yet all forms are born of causes and conditions, have no self-substance, and the functions that arise, like moon-in-water or flower-in-air, cannot be grasped. The Heart Sūtra says: “Form is emptiness, emptiness is form.” This says that form and emptiness are not two, neither being nor non-being. For all phenomenal situations are manifestations of the true-emptiness wondrous-substance, and the true-emptiness wondrous-substance likewise cannot exist apart from forms. For example, water raises waves; apart from the waves one cannot obtain water. In our practice, we must neither grasp forms as substantial and cling to them without letting go, nor be able to deviate from forms, discarding being to attach to emptiness. Therefore, whether we sit in meditation to establish concentration, or function in the post-meditation, we must be without grasping or discarding, so as to accord with the principle of the Middle Way and enter the great Way of true emptiness and wondrous being.

But because we still do not understand the principle of form and emptiness very well, I have above further set forth the meaning of form and emptiness, and quoted the recorded sayings of Chan Master Guifeng Zongmi, reaffirming the importance of recognizing the true mind; and I have spoken on the question of where a practitioner finally goes at the moment of death, so that everyone may enter into the gist of the Mahāmudrā, not take a detour in the practice, and go directly to the great Way of true emptiness and wondrous being.
Recognizing the Dharmakāya

blocks.text: 1. Clarifying the Coarse Delusions — Neither Grasping Nor Letting Loose

inline.s: Let us now return to the Mahāmudrā of the Ganges. Earlier we spoke of how the Mahāmudrā is an actual method that directly points us to the true mind. The Mahāmudrā is the one-real dharma-realm, is our true mind, is the substance that is without cultivation, without correction, without distraction. But to enter the experiential ground of the Mahāmudrā, at first one must also pass through a period of arduous cultivation. Without practice, you cannot recognize that the awareness apart from thought is the person’s own nature and accomplish the great Way. Why? The Mahāmudrā says:

What are the coarse delusions that turn with circumstances? When we give rise to mind on encountering objects and ceaselessly cling, seeing this and thinking of this, seeing that and thinking of that, unable to let go, in a jumble, topsy-turvy, idle brooding — this is called coarse delusion. The coarse delusion is like dark clouds covering the sun, covering the luminous original face of our mind; therefore it must be cut off. If the coarse delusion is not cut off, the practice does not get on the road. Why? When you are on the seat, all you have is topsy-turvy delusive thinking, thinking of this and that; off the seat you turn with circumstances, clinging ceaselessly; you absolutely cannot see the original face of the self-mind — this is wandering in birth and death! How can the practice ascend the road, how can it accomplish?

Where the true mind is, and what the true mind looks like, has been pointed out directly many times. If, after being directly pointed out, we still cannot see it, that shows our deluded mind is very heavy; then we should do the practice of cutting off the coarse delusion.

Enlightenment and realization of the Way have an order, and therefore the practice too has an order. How is it divided? At the beginning of the practice one must sever the coarse delusion that turns with circumstances. What is the coarse delusion? Seeing this and thinking of this, seeing that and thinking of that, giving rise to mind upon objects and clinging ceaselessly — that is called the coarse delusion. In our practice we pay no attention to it and let everything go — that is severing the coarse delusion. When the coarse delusion is severed, there still remains the subtle delusion, that is, certain thoughts in our mind. All of you who have practiced know that when we stop the coarse delusive thoughts, then the subtle thoughts, one after another, without our knowing, spring forth; this that springs forth is called the subtle delusion. In the Dharma-character school this is called “manas.” The five all-pervading mental factors that the Dharma-character school teaches, which everyone has, which all beings have — namely attention, contact, feeling, perception, and thought — these are the most fundamental deluded mind. The mind (manas) is the mind-root. It is always moving, like a submerged fish moving in the depths, and it moves very swiftly; on its surface you cannot see it moving, but it flows ceaselessly, without pause — this is the subtle, the extremely subtle delusive thought. This extremely subtle delusive thought is also called the subtle streaming. It is most subtle; in the place of utmost stillness, it is like water flowing at high speed — it looks as though it is not moving at all, but in fact it moves very swiftly, beyond what the eye can see. Only by entering the samādhi of Vajrasattva can one see it. Therefore after the coarse delusion is severed, there still remain the subtle, the fine, and the extremely fine delusions. How much less — when we first begin to practice, we have only achieved a motionless body. How can one see this extremely subtle delusive thought? Only by calming the mind and sitting in meditation, first clarifying the coarse delusions, can we see the subtle and extremely subtle delusive thoughts, and then sever them, realizing the original face of the self-mind. Therefore one must first break the coarse delusion.

How do we practice? The Mahāmudrā instructs us thus: “At first, let the mind abide in evenness, neither grasping nor letting loose.” At the outset of the practice, first let our mind be very even and calm, without attachment, without affliction, without constraint, without bondage — open, vast, and let it go. Confucianism says: “The gentleman is open and calm; the petty person is always anxious.” The petty person has profit and loss, gain and harm in his mind and turns in circles within it, anxious about loss, anxious about gain, and is therefore always anxious. The gentleman does not fret over gain or loss, regards everything indifferently, and is therefore open and calm. We who cultivate the Way are great gentlemen, great heroes, and all the more should be open and calm, letting everything go, even and without attachment. “Open and calm” means even and smooth, straight and straight, without any bending; the mind unbending — the straight mind is the place of practice. “Calm and vast” means sweeping everything entirely empty, without attachment; therefore it is free and at ease. The Mahāmudrā tells us to begin by doing this.

If one cannot do this, and there is some attachment, a turning ceaselessly in the mind, then we must apply a remedy according to the Dharma. How to remedy it? It is “neither grasping nor letting loose.” To grasp is to seize it, to hold it down; to let loose is to indulge it. We should neither seize it nor indulge it, but let it be natural. In our practice, if we seize the thought too tightly, afraid to move at all, then little by little it dies. But neither should we let a thought arise freely; otherwise we fall into indulgence, which is also wrong. When a thought comes, I pay it no attention — this is neither grasping nor letting loose.

In fact, in cultivating all dharmas we are simply training the practice of “paying no attention.” Thoughts do not fail to come; they do not fail to arise. Let them come, let them arise; pay them no attention, and they naturally dissolve. Whether reciting the Buddha-name, holding a mantra, or investigating chan, one must, when a thought comes, neither grasp nor let loose. In truth a thought cannot be seized or suppressed; it will come, just as the ancients said: when the wind stops the waves still surge. For one who recites the Buddha-name, when a thought comes, pay no attention to it, and raise the Buddha-name. For one who investigates chan, when a thought comes, pay no attention to it, and raise the huatou. For one who cultivates the esoteric path, when a thought comes, pay no attention to it, and raise the mantra. Single-mindedly tending the Buddha-name, single-mindedly tending the huatou, single-mindedly tending the mantra, the delusive thoughts are naturally transformed away. As for thoughts, it is not that one forbids them to rise, nor that one lets them run free; rather, one transforms them away — this is living, not dead. Earlier I mentioned the verse of Chan Master Wolun: “Wolun has a skill, he can cut off all thought; when mind meets objects it does not arise, and bodhi grows day by day.” That was suppressing thought so it does not arise — that is dead, and won’t do! It must be neither grasping nor letting loose — paying it no attention.

When a delusive thought comes, that is admittedly not good, but if you crush it to death, all is lost. For the delusive thought is born of the true mind, as waves arise from water. If you crush the delusive thought, just as when you eliminate the waves the water too is gone, then the true mind is no longer alive. We know the true mind is lively and vibrant, able to contain all things, able to produce all dharmas, able to rise to wondrous functions. If you truly crush the delusive thought, the true mind becomes wood, earth, metal, and stone, and can no longer perform wondrous functions.

Wood, earth, metal, and stone form one of the twelve classes of beings. Wood, earth, metal, and stone are without feeling. At first glance they seem unrelated to us, since we humans and all beings of the six realms of transmutation — devas, humans, asuras, hungry ghosts, animals, hells — all have feeling, all have sentient views and love. People are beings of feeling, while wood, earth, metal, and stone are dull and unfeeling, dead and motionless; they seem unrelated to us. But in fact this is not so. Though the twelve classes of beings are of various kinds, they are all one spiritual nature, all manifested from the one-real dharma-realm, of the same root and source as we humans; not a different class. The Buddha-nature is originally real and not false, able to produce all dharmas, and is the spiritual root complete with all wondrous functions. But because we cling to outer forms and are enveloped by ignorance, abiding in objects and cleaving to feelings, creating karma and receiving retribution, we lose the true mind, and the one-real is divided into inner and outer. The inner true is our own body and mind; the outer true is the mountains, rivers, great earth, sun, moon, stars, grasses and forests and other things outside — called things outside the body. In fact, all of these are ourselves! Because of ignorance, we take a small portion of the four elements — earth, water, fire, wind — and bind it within this fleshy husk as “self,” while ignoring the greater part of the four elements, regarding them as things outside the body. Thus there come to be the twelve classes of beings. In fact, with or without feeling, all share the one root. Therefore the scripture says: “Sentient and insentient alike are wholly the seed of wisdom.” The insentient too are ourselves! “Wholly the seed of wisdom” is the Buddha’s wisdom, is the wisdom of all kinds, is, on the one hand, knowing all the functions of all the Buddhas (that is, the Dharma of all the Buddhas, all of which one can completely know), and on the other hand, knowing the causal seeds of all beings.

Now, some people practicing have a little experience: a voice by the ear tells them what is about to happen, that someone is coming, and what he looks like — this is told by a “reporting spirit.” But some people think they have wisdom and supernatural powers, able to foresee who is coming and what will happen, and so preen themselves: Ah! How fine this is, I have foreknowledge. In fact it is not at all good! For this is a “transmitting ghost” at work. If you associate with it for a long time, you will be exploited by it and harmed by it. How does this ghost come to be? This person, while alive in the world, specialized in forming cliques for selfish ends, in abetting evil and stirring up litigation — that is, helping people do evil, helping people file lawsuits, plotting for wealth and harming life, and so on. He created hellish karma and therefore fell into hell to suffer. After the suffering of hell was over and he came out, his habitual tendency to form cliques and do evil throughout his former life still remained, and was moreover very heavy. Therefore he attaches to a person as his own body and tells people of future events. Hence he is called a transmitting ghost; he is no good thing.

In our practice, when we hear a voice by the ear telling us this or that, we must not suppose we have supernatural powers. That is not a good thing; that is a ghost! The scriptures speak of several kinds of ghosts. For example, greed for wealth: one who in life loved money and gold, the more the better, and because of greed did evil and fell into hell. After the suffering was over, his greedy habit remained: whatever he sees he wants, and when he meets grass and trees, he thinks they are very good, thinking they are himself. So he attaches to grass and trees to manifest spirits and do mischief. It is said that in Shanghai’s Fuxing Park there was a bodhi tree said to be very — how shall I say — efficacious, and everyone flocked to it, praying and worshiping, and all sorts of problems were solved; very efficacious. This was the mischief of a “strange ghost” attaching to grass and wood. There are also lecherous men and women; because lust is the fire of desire, when they fell into hell they were burned by the fire of desire. After the suffering ended and they came out, because lust is frivolous, they met the wind and took form, using the wind as their body — this is the “drought ghost,” that is, the female demon. There are also those who use great mountains and great water as their body — what ghost is this? It is called the “mountain-fiend,” that is, the ghost of wrong views. Because in their former lives their views were not correct; they were arrogant and self-important, thought themselves right, and when others held differing opinions, they resorted to secret schemes and cunning plots to harm others. Therefore they fell into hell. After the suffering ended, because of their arrogance and self-importance, they used the essence of sun and moon as their body, seizing the light of sun and moon, and attaching to mountains and water to manifest spirits. So everyone says this place is extremely efficacious. For instance, until recently there was far-flung talk of a “water-sprinkled Avalokiteshvara” in Hangzhou: on Ziyang Mountain there was a stone, ordinarily a smooth bare rock with nothing on it; but when water was poured on it, the image of Avalokiteshvara appeared, hence people called it the water-sprinkled Avalokiteshvara. People told one another that this place was incredibly efficacious, and everyone came from all directions to get water to drink, to cure all diseases. In fact this is a ghost that uses the essence of sun and moon as its body.

Thus it can be seen that all these ghosts, spirits, and even wood, earth, metal, and stone, are ourselves! For this reason it is said, “Sentient and insentient alike are wholly the seed of wisdom.” Our Buddha-nature is originally able to know the causal seeds of all beings, and also able to know the wondrous Dharma of all the Buddhas, the perfect, complete substance of great prajñā.
